tagline.text: A museum that brings the life of Chinese Filipinos to life with wax figures

location.label: Location
location.text: 32 Anda Street (corner of Cabildo Street), Intramuros, Manila

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (indoor museum, open year-round)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–600 (per person, covering admission, transport and snacks)

children.text: Bahay Tsinoy is a museum of Chinese-Filipino history in Intramuros that tells the story of centuries of Chinese and Filipino life together through wax figures and artifacts. The three-story building is air-conditioned, so it makes a good break on a hot day of walking around Intramuros.

Bahay Tsinoy is a museum whose Tagalog name means "House of the Tsinoy," and its official name is the Museum of Chinese in Philippine Life. It stands at 32 Anda Street, on the corner where it meets Cabildo Street, in Intramuros, Manila. In the Philippines, "Tsinoy" refers to Filipinos of Chinese descent. The museum was created to show how Chinese Filipinos have lived and what they have contributed to Philippine history and everyday life. Chinese Filipinos are often thought of only as merchants, but here you will meet a much wider range of people: those who took part in the fight for independence, craftsmen, porcelain traders and national leaders. It is also a chance to trace the Chinese influence that has seeped into Philippine food, names and family customs.

The museum was conceived by the civic group Kaisa Para sa Kaunlaran and built with support from the Angelo King Foundation and donations from the community. The building was designed in 1996 and is generally said to have opened in 1999. It is a three-story, American Colonial-style building. The same building also houses the Chinben See Memorial Library and the Awat Keng Auditorium, so it serves as a cultural center for the Chinese-Filipino community. The building is also known as the Kaisa-Angelo King Heritage Center, so try both names when you search on a map app. Details such as the opening year differ slightly between sources. The design is said to be the work of architect Eva Penamora together with the late Honrado Fernandez.

The exhibits follow a timeline. Rooms cover early trade before Spanish colonization, the Chinese quarter known as the Parian, colonial culture, life in the 1800s, Chinese-Filipino heroes who fought for independence, and finally today's leaders. The near life-size wax dioramas are especially worth seeing. Figures such as a barber, a food peddler, a goldsmith and a cobbler stand in period scenes, and one room recreates an entire 1800s household with Chinese-style furniture and a bed. The captions are mainly in English and easy to follow, and eye-catching touches such as the terracotta warrior replica at the entrance keep children from getting bored.

Bahay Tsinoy is within walking distance of San Agustin Church, Manila Cathedral and Fort Santiago. Allow an hour or two to read the exhibits. Confirm opening hours and the child rate with the museum and check admissions separately for the nearby heritage sites you plan to visit.

This exhibit covers the Parian, the district where Chinese people lived in Spanish-era Manila, and the trade history that came before it. Maps and artifacts show how Chinese and local people interacted for a very long time, and seeing it before you walk around Intramuros makes the city look different.

Occupations of the time, such as a barber, a food peddler, a goldsmith and a cobbler, are recreated with near life-size figures. One room moves an entire Chinese-Filipino household of the 1800s into the museum, so you can see the furniture and everyday tools up close. Follow the on-site rules when taking photos.

blocks.title: The independence movement and the Martyrs' Hall

children.text: The Martyrs' Hall honors Chinese-Filipino heroes who fought for the freedom of the Philippines, and the exhibit "In Defense of Freedom" tells that story. Many travelers learn for the first time that people of Chinese descent took part in the Philippine revolution, and this is often where visitors linger longest.

This room displays ceramics excavated in the Philippines dating from the 10th to the 17th centuries, showing that Chinese porcelain reached the archipelago very long ago. A shell collection is also on display, so even family members with different tastes will find something to see.

This exhibit gathers old prints and photographs, showing old Manila and Chinese-Filipino streets. It documents how the city changed during the Spanish and American periods, and it is worth a look if you are interested in photography or history.

This exhibit introduces people of Chinese descent who made their mark in Philippine politics, business and society. The hall "Tsinoys in Nation-Building," added in 2004, continues the theme with people who have contributed to modern society.

blocks.title: The hologram in the dark room at the end

children.text: Near the end of the tour there is a dimly lit section where a hologram of a Tsinoy tells how early Chinese settlers blended into Philippine society. Young children may be startled, so let them know in advance.

The building houses the Chinben See Memorial Library (about 8,000 items) and the Awat Keng Auditorium with about 380 seats. The library and research area keep their own opening hours, so ask in advance if you want to use research materials.

items.title: Half-day Intramuros route
items.subtitle: Museum visit and a walk through the walled city

children.text: Take a taxi or Grab from your Manila hotel to Intramuros and head to Bahay Tsinoy at 32 Anda Street. If the doors are not open yet, stroll the nearby walled streets.
See the terracotta warrior replica at the entrance and buy your ticket. Go through the exhibits slowly, from early contacts to the Parian, colonial culture and life in the 1800s.
After the independence exhibit, the Martyrs' Hall and the gallery of national leaders, finish in the ceramics room.
Have lunch inside Intramuros and walk toward San Agustin Church.
Visit one more place, either Manila Cathedral or Fort Santiago, and return to your hotel by taxi or Grab as the day cools.
Intramuros is very hot at midday. Plan outdoor stretches for the morning or late afternoon and put indoor stops such as the museum in the middle of the day.
Set out from your hotel and start with the sites in Intramuros that open earliest.
At Bahay Tsinoy, see the exhibits your children will like first, focusing on the dioramas and the dark hologram room.
After lunch, rest and look around a nearby church inside and out.
Take a taxi to the museum on Roxas Boulevard so your children have time to run around.
It takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
by taxi or Grab from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Intramuros. This varies a lot with traffic, so allow extra time.
If you are staying at a hotel in Manila, Intramuros is usually within
10–30 minutes
by taxi.
Check the exact fare and travel time locally when you arrive from the airport.

On LRT-1 (the yellow line), the closest station is Central Terminal, about a 12-minute walk (2026 guides). From Carriedo Station it is about a 19-minute walk, and older guides also describe boarding a jeepney bound for the Pier in front of Santa Cruz Church and getting off in front of Bahay Tsinoy. Jeepney routes can change, so confirm locally.
Jeepney routes can change, so ask the driver or people nearby for "Bahay Tsinoy in Intramuros" and get off there.
Walking is the main way to get around inside Intramuros, and there are also tricycles, tourist bicycle taxis and horse-drawn kalesa carriages.

First-time visitors will find it easy to take Grab to a spot near the museum entrance. Roads inside the walls may be one-way or restricted, so your driver may drop you off near the entrance, in which case find the building with your map app and walk.
Bahay Tsinoy is an air-conditioned indoor museum, so you can visit any time of year. If you also want to walk around Intramuros, the drier and cooler dry season is better.

Around the Lunar New Year, events are held in places such as Binondo in Manila, which makes it a good time to experience Chinese-Filipino culture as well. The city is crowded then, so allow plenty of travel time.

There are hotels inside Intramuros as well, but most travelers stay in Ermita, Malate or Makati and take a taxi in. If the museum is your main reason for visiting, staying in the city makes getting around easier. Hotel names and prices change a lot from season to season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

Inside and near Intramuros you will find Spanish-style restaurants, Filipino restaurants and cafes. Walking toward San Agustin Church after the museum brings you to many good lunch spots. On very hot days, stop at a cool cafe before or after your visit for water and a snack, and choose market food in Intramuros only after checking the hygiene with your own eyes. Binondo Chinatown is close by, so trying dumplings and noodles there is an enjoyable experience that ties in with the museum's theme.

The air conditioning keeps it cool inside, so bring a light jacket.
The streets of Intramuros are uneven, so wear comfortable shoes.
If you are visiting with children, explain the dark hologram room to them beforehand.
The library and research room keep different hours from the museum, so inquire separately if you want to use them.
Exhibit captions are mainly in English, so a translation app can help. Ask at the entrance whether photography is allowed.
The nearby churches and fort close at different times, so check your route in advance.
Opening hours and fees differ by source, so you may make the trip for nothing. Check with the museum right before you go.
The museum may be closed on Mondays or public holidays, so check the day before.
Watch for pickpockets and touts on the streets of Intramuros and keep valuables in front of you.
The outdoors is very hot at midday. Bring water and a hat and mix indoor and outdoor plans.
Some exhibits may or may not be open, so treat the information in this guide as what could be confirmed in 2026 and check the latest announcements.
The Spanish-era walled city where Bahay Tsinoy stands. You can explore its walls, churches and fort on foot.
A few minutes away on foot, this is one of the oldest stone churches in the Philippines and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A fort at the northern end of Intramuros, well known as the prison where José Rizal was held.
A short taxi ride away, the world's oldest Chinatown offers food and streets that tie in with the museum's theme.
